**On-policy learning evaluates or improves the policy generating the data; off-policy learning targets a policy that can differ from the data-generating behavior.** This distinction is about the relationship between policies, not simply whether a replay buffer exists. [1](https://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html)

Let $\mu$ be the behavior policy and $\pi$ the target policy. In on-policy learning, the data are generated by the relevant current policy. In off-policy learning, data may come from an exploratory policy, an older policy, or a fixed logged dataset while the algorithm learns about $\pi$.

SARSA uses the next action actually sampled by the behavior policy:

$$Q(s,a)\leftarrow Q(s,a)+\alpha[r+\gamma Q(s',a')-Q(s,a)].$$

With matched behavior and target policies, this is on-policy. Q-learning instead uses $r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$, targeting greedy action values while behavior may still explore. In a hazardous environment, SARSA can account for the cost of continuing exploration, whereas the greedy target assumes future greedy choices. [1](https://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html)

Importance sampling can correct expectations from behavior to target using ratios $\pi(a\mid s)/\mu(a\mid s)$. The support requirement is essential: if the target may choose an action that behavior never chooses, the necessary evidence is absent. Products of ratios over long trajectories can also have enormous variance.

**Off-policy is not synonymous with offline.** An off-policy agent can keep collecting fresh experience online while learning from replay. Offline RL forbids new interaction during training, making distribution shift especially difficult. Likewise, an algorithm described as approximately on-policy may reuse a bounded amount of recent data with explicit corrections; inspect its objective rather than relying only on the label. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.01643)[4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347)

In an interview, specify who generated the data, which policy the update targets, and what assumptions justify reuse. In tabular settings some algorithms have convergence guarantees under conditions such as sufficient exploration and suitable step sizes. Function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy data together can destabilize learning, so those tabular guarantees should not be transferred uncritically to deep networks.
